claims.text: Adding approximately 5 at.% Hf to nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 will suppress radiation-induced Cr–V-rich precipitate formation near 8 dpa.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain the low irradiation-induced hardening of the unmodified alloy.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain high radiation resistance.
Adding approximately 5 at.% Hf will not sacrifice practical bulk manufacturability.
Powder processing can produce nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 with a uniform fine-grained pre-irradiation microstructure.
Hf can be homogeneously distributed in the alloy during powder processing.
Hf will segregate to grain boundaries and irradiation-induced defect sinks.
Hf segregation will modify local chemistry and reduce Cr and V supersaturation.
Reduced Cr and V supersaturation will hinder clustering into Cr–V-rich precipitates.
Hf segregation will stabilize grain boundaries and maintain nanocrystalline stability during irradiation.
Hf at defect sinks will inhibit the local solute partitioning responsible for Cr–V-rich precipitate nucleation.
Hf microalloying will provide additional sites for irradiation-defect recombination.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 forms Cr–V-rich precipitates under energetic-particle exposure near 8 dpa.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits dislocation loops and slight hardening near 8 dpa.
At approximately 8 dpa and 500°C, the Hf-doped alloy will show a marked reduction or absence of Cr–V-rich precipitates relative to the baseline.
At approximately 8 dpa and 500°C, the Hf-doped alloy will have irradiation-induced hardening similar to the baseline.
At approximately 8 dpa and 500°C, the Hf-doped alloy will have dislocation-loop densities comparable to the baseline.
At doses much higher than 8 dpa or temperatures substantially different from 500°C, alternative damage mechanisms or different Hf segregation behavior may occur.
